title: Structured Lifestyle Changes Improved Brain Health by 55% in At-Risk Adults, Landmark AAIC Study Shows
excerpt: The LatAm-FINGERS trial, presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference 2026 in London and published in The Lancet, found that coached exercise, adapted diets, cognitive training, and social engagement dramatically boosted memory and thinking in older adults across 11 countries.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Structured lifestyle changes improved brain health by 55% in at-risk older adults.
  • The LatAm-FINGERS trial involved over 1,000 participants across 11 Latin American countries.
  • Participants received coaching in exercise, diet, cognitive training, and social engagement.
  • The study highlights the importance of structure and social support for cognitive health.
  • Alzheimer's Association invested over $81 million in related programs and initiatives.
Impact of Structured Lifestyle Changes

Source: Alzheimer's Association, The Lancet
A two-year clinical trial involving more than 1,000 older adults across 11 Latin American countries has delivered some of the strongest evidence yet that structured lifestyle interventions can meaningfully improve brain health in people at risk of dementia — and the findings have direct implications for South Asian communities facing similar cognitive health threats. The LatAm-FINGERS study, presented on July 13 at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference (AAIC) 2026 in London and simultaneously published in *The Lancet*, found that participants who received ongoing coaching, supervised exercise, nutrition counseling based on an adapted MIND diet, computerized cognitive training, and regular group meetings showed 55 percent greater improvement in global cognition compared to those who received only periodic health education. ## The Study Design Researchers enrolled 1,065 participants across 12 sites in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Mexico, Peru, and Uruguay. All participants were at risk of cognitive decline based on age and health factors. They were randomly assigned to one of two groups. The Systematic Lifestyle Intervention (SLI) group of 539 participants received structured, ongoing support: supervised exercise programs that incorporated culturally familiar activities like salsa and tango, nutrition counseling that adapted the MIND diet using local foods like quinoa, açaí, and chia seeds, computerized cognitive training sessions, cardiovascular risk monitoring, and 38 group meetings over two years for social connection and accountability. The Flexible Lifestyle Intervention (FLI) group of 526 participants received periodic health education and general recommendations with only four group meetings over the same period — no ongoing coaching or supervision. > **"POINTER formula can be adapted for anybody." ## The Bigger Picture The Alzheimer's Association has invested more than $81 million in the LatAm-FINGERS and U.S."** After two years, the coached group significantly outperformed the self-guided group across every cognitive measure: memory, executive function, and processing speed. ## Why South Asians Should Pay Attention The study's central finding — that *structure* and *social support* are what make lifestyle interventions work — carries particular weight for South Asian diaspora communities. ![The Lancet — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/3/38/The_Lancet_cover%2C_2_March_2019.jpg) South Asians are already at elevated risk for several of the conditions that accelerate cognitive decline: type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome. The MASALA study from Northwestern University has documented how these risk factors cluster in South Asian Americans by midlife, even among those reporting healthier behaviors. Each of these conditions is a known contributor to dementia risk.
Key Components of the Intervention
›Supervised exercise programs with culturally familiar activities.
›Nutrition counseling based on adapted MIND diet.
›Computerized cognitive training sessions.
›Regular group meetings for social connection.
Yet the cultural infrastructure for structured health interventions already exists in diaspora communities. Temple-based yoga groups, walking groups in suburban neighborhoods, multigenerational households that naturally provide social engagement — these parallel the very elements the LatAm-FINGERS study found most effective. The challenge is formalizing them with coaching, dietary guidance, and cognitive exercises. "We did not simply translate the U.S. POINTER model into Spanish and Portuguese," said lead author Lucia Crivelli, Ph.D., of Fleni, a neurological institute in Buenos Aires. "We adapted it to local cultures and habits while preserving its core elements — making the program practical, affordable, and feasible as a public health strategy." Laura D. Baker, Ph.D., the U.S. POINTER principal investigator at Wake Forest University, added: "We now have a second strong finding in a completely different part of the world, which suggests that the U.S. POINTER formula can be adapted for anybody." ## The Bigger Picture The Alzheimer's Association has invested more than $81 million in the LatAm-FINGERS and U.S. POINTER programs. The organization has launched several public initiatives based on these findings, including a Brain Health Habit Builder assessment tool and the (re)think your brain initiative, which helps people translate brain health awareness into daily action. Both studies are part of the World-Wide FINGERS network, based on the original Finnish FINGER trial that first demonstrated the potential of multidomain lifestyle interventions for cognitive protection. The network now spans more than 45 countries. With dementia rates rising globally and no cure on the horizon, the message from AAIC 2026 is as practical as it is urgent: the most effective brain health strategy currently available is not a drug — it is a coached combination of exercise, diet, mental stimulation, and human connection.

For a diaspora community already rich in many of these traditions, the barrier may be less about adoption and more about organization. *Findings were presented at AAIC 2026 in London and published simultaneously in The Lancet. Sources: Alzheimer's Association, PR Newswire.*
